metadata.title: De La Riva Guard Bottom | BJJ Position Guide | BJJ Graph
metadata.description: Master De La Riva Guard Bottom in BJJ. Complete guide covering sweeps, back takes, and leg attacks. Open guard position with 65% sweep success rate at advanced level.

overview:
De La Riva Guard Bottom is one of the most dynamic and versatile open guard positions in modern Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu. Named after Ricardo De La Riva who revolutionized its use in the 1980s, this position is characterized by the bottom player hooking their opponent's leg from the outside while controlling the opposite sleeve or collar. The De La Riva hook, created by threading your leg around the outside of your opponent's near leg and hooking behind their knee, creates powerful off-balancing opportunities and serves as the foundation for numerous sweeps, back takes, and leg entanglements.

This position excels at disrupting your opponent's base and posture, making it difficult for them to establish effective pressure or initiate guard passes. The De La Riva hook combined with strategic grips allows the bottom player to control distance, create angles, and threaten multiple attack sequences simultaneously. The position's effectiveness stems from its ability to break down the opponent's structure while maintaining offensive options - when executed properly, it forces the top player into a defensive posture rather than allowing them to dictate the pace of the engagement.

De La Riva Guard Bottom has become fundamental to competitive BJJ, particularly in no-gi grappling where it transitions seamlessly into leg lock systems and back attacks. The position offers exceptional versatility, allowing practitioners to chain together sweeps, transitions to other guards (X-Guard, Single Leg X), and direct paths to dominant positions like the back or mount. Its modern applications, influenced by practitioners like the Mendes brothers, Cobrinha, and the Miyao brothers, have expanded the position's scope to include berimbolo entries, kiss of the dragon variations, and sophisticated leg entanglement systems.
state_invariants: Bottom player's outside leg threaded around opponent's near leg with foot hooking behind their knee, creating the signature De La Riva hook that controls their base and prevents forward pressure
Bottom player controlling opponent's opposite sleeve or collar with a cross grip, creating a diagonal control system that disrupts their posture and enables angular attacks
Bottom player's other leg (non-hooking leg) positioned on opponent's hip, bicep, or knee to manage distance and prevent them from settling their weight or establishing smash passing pressure
Bottom player's hips angled away from opponent with shoulders off the mat, maintaining mobility and the ability to invert or change angles for sweeps and transitions
Opponent forced to maintain upright posture on their knees or in combat base, unable to flatten out or establish heavy top pressure due to the hook and grip configuration
prerequisites: Opponent in open guard passing position on their knees or in combat base
Bottom player has established the De La Riva hook around opponent's near leg
Bottom player has secured a cross grip on opponent's opposite sleeve, collar, or lapel
Bottom player's hips are mobile and not flattened to the mat
Sufficient space exists between players to allow for hook insertion and maintenance
key_principles: Maintain constant tension on the De La Riva hook by pulling your knee toward your chest and driving your hooking foot into the back of their knee
Create diagonal control by combining the hook with a strong cross grip to break down their posture and prevent them from squaring up to you
Use your non-hooking leg actively to manage distance - placing it on their hip, knee, or bicep to prevent them from closing distance and smashing forward
Keep your hips mobile and shoulders slightly off the mat to enable quick angle changes, inversions, and transitions to other positions
Constantly off-balance your opponent by pulling with your grips while extending and retracting the De La Riva hook to disrupt their base
Chain attacks together - if one sweep or transition is defended, immediately flow to the next option without resetting to neutral
Protect your non-hooking leg from being controlled or trapped, as losing this leg makes it difficult to recover and execute techniques

common_errors.error: Allowing the De La Riva hook to go slack or releasing tension on the opponent's trapped leg
common_errors.consequence: Opponent can easily step back and clear the hook, eliminating your primary control mechanism and allowing them to pass
common_errors.correction: Maintain constant pulling pressure with your hooking leg by keeping your knee pulled toward your chest and actively driving your foot into the back of their knee

common_errors.error: Losing the cross grip on the opponent's far sleeve or collar
common_errors.consequence: Without the diagonal control system, opponent can square up their posture, establish better base, and pass with pressure
common_errors.correction: Fight aggressively for the cross grip and if broken, immediately re-establish it or transition to a different guard position

common_errors.error: Allowing your non-hooking leg to be controlled or trapped by the opponent
common_errors.consequence: Losing your free leg makes it nearly impossible to maintain distance, change angles, or execute sweeps and transitions
common_errors.correction: Keep your non-hooking leg active and mobile, constantly repositioning it on their hip, bicep, or knee to maintain control of distance

common_errors.error: Staying static in one configuration without threatening attacks or changing angles
common_errors.consequence: Opponent can settle into a defensive position, work on clearing your hooks methodically, and eventually pass your guard
common_errors.correction: Constantly chain attacks together, move your hips to create new angles, and threaten multiple techniques to keep opponent reactive

common_errors.error: Flattening your back completely to the mat and losing hip mobility
common_errors.consequence: Cannot execute inversions, berimbolo entries, or quick angle changes that make De La Riva guard effective
common_errors.correction: Keep your shoulders slightly elevated off the mat and maintain active hip movement to enable dynamic transitions

common_errors.error: Inserting the De La Riva hook without first establishing proper grips and distance management
common_errors.consequence: Opponent can immediately counter by driving forward, smashing the guard, or establishing dominant grips before you're ready
common_errors.correction: Establish your grips and distance control first, then insert the hook when you have proper control of the engagement

common_errors.error: Overcommitting to one technique without having backup options prepared
common_errors.consequence: When the initial attack is defended, you're left in a weakened position with no clear path forward
common_errors.correction: Always have at least two or three options chained together based on how opponent reacts to your initial attack

training_drills.name: De La Riva Hook Retention Drill
training_drills.description: Partner attempts to clear your De La Riva hook using various methods (stepping back, circling, driving forward) while you maintain the hook and grips. Focus on keeping constant tension and re-establishing the hook if temporarily cleared. 3-minute rounds switching roles.

training_drills.name: Sweep Chain Flow Drill
training_drills.description: Starting from De La Riva guard, flow through a sequence of sweeps based on partner's reactions: attempt the basic De La Riva sweep, if defended flow to waiter sweep, then to overhead sweep, then to balloon sweep. Partner provides progressive resistance. Focus on smooth transitions between techniques without resetting to neutral.

training_drills.name: Berimbolo Entry Repetitions
training_drills.description: Practice entering the berimbolo from De La Riva guard with partner providing 50% resistance. Focus on timing the entry when opponent drives forward, maintaining the De La Riva hook throughout the inversion, and coming up to back control. Perform 10 repetitions per side, then switch roles.

training_drills.name: Transition Network Drill
training_drills.description: Start in De La Riva guard and flow between De La Riva, X-Guard, Single Leg X, and Reverse De La Riva based on partner's position and pressure. Partner moves between different passing positions (standing, kneeling, pressure passing) while you adapt your guard. Focus on seamless transitions and maintaining offensive control.

training_drills.name: Grip Fighting from De La Riva
training_drills.description: Partner actively fights to break your cross grip and establish their own dominant grips while you maintain the De La Riva hook and work to secure and maintain your preferred grips. Focus on re-gripping quickly when grips are broken and using the hook to off-balance opponent during grip exchanges.

expert_insights.danaher: The De La Riva guard represents a fundamental shift in guard theory - from using the guard purely as a defensive shield to employing it as an active weapons system for off-balancing and attacking. The biomechanical genius of the position lies in its exploitation of human anatomy's vulnerability to rotational forces applied to the knee joint. By threading your leg around the outside of your opponent's leg and hooking behind their knee, you create a powerful lever that disrupts their sagittal plane stability while your cross grip eliminates their frontal plane balance. This diagonal control system - hook on one side, grip on the opposite side - creates what I call 'structural breakdown through diagonal tension.' The opponent cannot move forward because of the hook, cannot move backward because you're pulling them, and cannot rotate because the cross grip prevents it. Understanding this principle allows you to chain techniques not randomly, but systematically based on which plane of movement your opponent attempts to use for escape. When they try to remove the hook by stepping back, you have overhead and waiter sweeps. When they drive forward to smash, you have berimbolo and kiss of the dragon. Every defensive reaction opens a specific offensive opportunity, making De La Riva guard a perfect example of using physics and biomechanics to overcome strength disadvantages.
expert_insights.gordon_ryan: De La Riva guard is one of the highest-percentage positions in modern competitive jiu-jitsu because it gives you multiple paths to dominant positions and submissions while being extremely difficult for opponents to pass cleanly. In my competition experience, I've found the key to making De La Riva truly dangerous is being relentlessly offensive with it - you can't just hold the position and wait. I'm constantly threatening the berimbolo, the sweep, or transitioning to X-guard or Single Leg X. The moment you become defensive or static in De La Riva, good passers will methodically clear your hooks and pass. What makes it especially effective at the highest levels is that it works both gi and no-gi, and it creates immediate access to leg entanglements which is crucial in modern competitive grappling. When someone stands to disengage, I'm immediately entering outside ashi or saddle positions. The position also has excellent synergy with modern back attack systems - the berimbolo has become one of the most high-percentage back takes in competition because it's so difficult to defend when executed properly. I've won numerous matches by chaining De La Riva sweeps into immediate mount or back attacks, then finishing with submissions. The versatility is what makes it championship-level - you're never stuck with only one option, you always have multiple attack paths based on how opponent reacts.
expert_insights.eddie_bravo: De La Riva guard is sick because it's one of those positions that proves jiu-jitsu is constantly evolving. Ricardo De La Riva basically invented a whole new guard system that nobody was using before, and now it's fundamental to the game. What I love about it is how it opens up these crazy inversion entries and back takes that look like magic to people who don't understand the mechanics. The berimbolo is basically a De La Riva specialty - you're using that hook to control their base while you spin underneath them and come up on their back. It's like a skateboard trick but for jiu-jitsu. In the 10th Planet system, we've adapted De La Riva concepts for no-gi by focusing more on the leg entanglement side of things. Without the gi grips, you have to be more aggressive about getting to outside ashi or inside position on the legs. We also combine De La Riva with rubber guard concepts when the distance closes - if they break your hook and try to smash, you can transition to mission control or invisible collar. The key innovation we've brought is treating De La Riva not as a standalone position but as an entry system to our other guards and leg attacks. It's like a highway interchange - you can use it to get to X-guard, to single leg X, to leg locks, or to the truck position. That versatility combined with the ability to completely off-balance and frustrate passers makes it essential for any modern no-gi game.

overview:
De La Riva Guard (DLR) is a sophisticated open guard variation where the bottom player hooks the opponent's lead leg with their outside foot while controlling the ankle or pant with their hand on the same side. The other hand typically controls the opponent's sleeve or collar, creating a structure that limits the opponent's mobility and generates powerful sweeping leverage. This guard has become fundamental in modern BJJ, particularly for setting up berimbolo sequences, back takes, and creating connections to other guard systems.

Developed by Ricardo De La Riva in the 1980s as a counter to the traditional standing guard pass, this position revolutionized modern guard play by introducing a systematic approach to controlling the opponent's base from an off-angle relationship. The DLR hook creates a powerful mechanical advantage that disrupts the opponent's weight distribution and limits their passing options, forcing them into predictable responses that can be exploited through sweeps, back takes, or transitions to other guard systems. The position's effectiveness lies in its ability to create constant threats while maintaining defensive security, making it a cornerstone of contemporary competitive BJJ at all belt levels.
state_invariants: Outside foot hooking behind opponent's lead leg, wrapping around their knee or thigh with the blade of the foot or instep creating tension and disrupting their base
Same-side hand controlling the ankle or pant grip of the hooked leg with firm tension, preventing the opponent from extracting their leg or establishing a stable stance
Opposite hand securing a grip on the opponent's sleeve, collar, or wrist, pulling their upper body down or to the side to break their posture and limit their mobility
Bottom player's hips are active and slightly elevated off the mat, angled away from the opponent to create leverage and prevent them from squaring up or applying direct pressure
Free leg positioned to block the opponent's opposite hip, push off for sweeps, or transition to other guards, maintaining dynamic mobility and threat potential

Understanding of off-balancing mechanics and leverage principles
Basic grip fighting fundamentals and hand control strategies
Adequate hamstring flexibility to maintain hook position
Ability to maintain active engagement while on back
key_principles: Control opponent's lead leg with both foot hook and hand grip, creating a two-point connection that limits their mobility
Maintain active grip on sleeve or collar to disrupt posture and prevent opponent from generating forward pressure
Create and manipulate angles constantly to keep opponent off-balance and vulnerable to sweeps
Keep hips mobile and elevated to prevent opponent from smashing through or establishing heavy top pressure
Coordinate upper and lower body controls to create complete positional dominance and offensive opportunities
Maintain proper distance management to prevent close-range pressure while staying connected enough to threaten sweeps
Use hook tension actively rather than passively to control opponent's weight distribution and base

common_errors.error: Passive hook placement without active tension
common_errors.consequence: Allows opponent to easily disengage and extract their leg, eliminating all offensive threat and control
common_errors.correction: Maintain constant active tension through the DLR hook by pulling the knee toward you while keeping your foot tightly wrapped, creating a biomechanical connection that restricts their movement

common_errors.error: Poor distance management allowing opponent too close
common_errors.consequence: Enables opponent to apply heavy top pressure, smash through the guard, or establish dominant passing positions
common_errors.correction: Use your free leg to maintain optimal distance by framing against their hip or shoulder, adjusting distance dynamically based on their movement patterns

common_errors.error: Static hip positioning without continuous adjustment
common_errors.consequence: Reduces sweeping power and allows opponent to settle into stable passing positions
common_errors.correction: Keep hips mobile and constantly adjust angles by rotating your body and elevating hips off the mat, creating off-balancing angles that amplify sweep effectiveness

common_errors.error: Neglecting upper body control with weak or absent grips
common_errors.consequence: Opponent can maintain strong posture and control distance, negating the effectiveness of the DLR hook
common_errors.correction: Establish and maintain firm collar or sleeve grips immediately when securing the hook, using grip fighting to break their posture and pull them into vulnerable positions

common_errors.error: Over-reliance on the hook without transitioning when compromised
common_errors.consequence: Results in being stuck in a weakened position as opponent successfully counters or passes
common_errors.correction: Develop fluid transitions to X-Guard, Single Leg X, or Reverse DLR when the primary DLR position is threatened, treating DLR as part of a dynamic guard retention system

common_errors.error: Insufficient leg dexterity in hook placement and control
common_errors.consequence: Hook slips or loses effectiveness, allowing easy escape and guard passing opportunities
common_errors.correction: Practice isolated hook drills to develop precise foot and leg control, focusing on maintaining hook depth and angle even under pressure

expert_insights.danaher: De La Riva Guard represents a fundamental shift in guard philosophy from passive protection to active disruption of the opponent's base and movement. The mechanical advantage created by the DLR hook is not merely about holding the leg, but about creating a fulcrum that amplifies your hip movement into powerful off-balancing forces. The systematic approach requires understanding the relationship between hook depth, grip configuration, and hip angle—when these three elements align properly, the guard becomes nearly impossible to pass without making critical errors. The key insight is that DLR functions as a hub position connecting to X-Guard, Single Leg X, and leg entanglement systems, making it essential to develop fluid transitions rather than viewing it as an isolated position. My emphasis is on creating clear defensive hierarchies when the position is threatened, ensuring you always have a systematic pathway to guard retention or advantageous transitions.
expert_insights.gordon_ryan: In competition, De La Riva Guard is primarily a transitional position rather than a static control—I use it to create immediate threats that force opponent reactions, then capitalize on those reactions with sweeps or back takes. The reality is that modern guard passers have developed sophisticated DLR counters, so you need to be explosive and decisive with your attacks rather than waiting in the position. My approach focuses on the berimbolo and Kiss of the Dragon as high-percentage paths to the back, but only when executed with precise timing as the opponent commits to their pass. The grip fighting phase before establishing DLR is actually more important than the position itself—if you can't secure a strong collar tie or sleeve grip first, the hook alone won't generate enough control. I often use DLR as a bait position, appearing to commit to it while actually setting up transitions to leg entanglements or X-Guard based on how they defend.
expert_insights.eddie_bravo: The beauty of De La Riva principles is how they translate to no-gi grappling when you adapt the mechanics rather than just removing the grips. In the 10th Planet system, we use ankle control and overhooks to create similar off-balancing dynamics without relying on gi grips, often combining DLR-style hooks with lockdown or rubber guard concepts to create hybrid positions that confuse traditional guard passers. The hook itself is universal—it works with or without the gi—but the real innovation comes from exploring unconventional grip configurations and combining DLR mechanics with calf slicer threats or truck entries. I love how DLR creates natural pathways to the twister system through berimbolo-style inversion, showing that seemingly different systems are actually connected through shared biomechanical principles. The key is developing comfort with being inverted and using your legs as primary control instruments rather than just defensive barriers.

metadata.title: De La Riva Guard Top | BJJ Position Guide | BJJ Graph
metadata.description: Master De La Riva Guard Top passing in BJJ. Complete guide covering hook removal, pressure strategies, and modern passing systems. Expert insights included.

overview:
De La Riva Guard Top position occurs when the top practitioner is facing an opponent playing De La Riva (DLR) guard, where the bottom player has their outside leg hooked behind the top player's near leg while controlling the pants or ankle, with their other leg typically managing distance or controlling the opposite side. The top player's goal is to neutralize the DLR hooks and leg controls, pass the guard, and establish a dominant position. This requires understanding DLR mechanics, applying appropriate pressure, and choosing the right passing strategy based on the bottom player's grips and positioning.

De La Riva guard is one of the most popular and effective open guards in modern BJJ, making DLR passing a critical skill for any serious competitor. The position presents unique challenges because the DLR hook creates off-balancing and sweeping threats while the opponent maintains distance control. Top players must balance maintaining good posture and base while simultaneously dismantling the guard structure. Modern DLR passing has evolved to include pressure-based approaches, mobile passing strategies, and combination techniques that address multiple DLR variations. Success requires systematic understanding of hook mechanics, grip fighting expertise, and the ability to chain multiple passing sequences when the initial attack is defended.
state_invariants: Bottom player has DLR hook active behind top player's leg, creating off-balancing leverage with their shin or foot pressuring behind the knee or thigh, establishing the fundamental mechanical disadvantage for the top player

Bottom player maintains distance control through legs or grips, typically controlling the top player's ankle, pants, or belt with their hands while their free leg creates frames or distance management, preventing immediate passing pressure

Top player is standing or in combat base with weight distributed through legs and maintaining upright posture to resist forward sweeps, with chest elevated and hips positioned back from the danger zone

Top player working to neutralize guard and pass, actively fighting grips and positioning to remove the DLR hook while preventing opponent from establishing perpendicular hip angle that maximizes sweeping leverage

Position is dynamic with constant adjustments as bottom player attempts to off-balance and top player seeks to establish passing grips and pressure, creating a chess match of grip fighting and positional warfare
prerequisites: Understanding of DLR guard mechanics and sweep threats including berimbolo, waiter sweep, and forward sweeps that exploit the hook's off-balancing power
Good base and balance to resist off-balancing, particularly against forward pressure from the DLR hook combined with ankle grip pulling force
Grip fighting skills to strip or control the ankle/pants grip that powers DLR control, as this grip is essential to the guard's effectiveness
Multiple passing strategies for different DLR variations including reverse DLR, single leg X transitions, and X-guard entries that bottom player may use defensively
Ability to recognize and defend berimbolo entries, which represent the highest-percentage back take threat from DLR guard
Understanding of pressure application timing to capitalize on moments when the DLR hook is compromised or removed
key_principles: Posture Maintenance: Stay upright with chest elevated and hips back to prevent forward sweeps and maintain balance against the DLR hook's off-balancing attempts
Grip Fighting: Strip or control the ankle/pants grip that powers DLR control, as this grip combined with the hook creates the primary sweeping mechanism
Hook Removal: Neutralize the DLR hook through pressure, leg positioning, or strategic movement to remove the bottom player's primary control point
Hip Control: Don't allow bottom player to maintain optimal hip angle perpendicular to you, as this angle maximizes their sweeping power and berimbolo entries
Pressure Application: Once hooks are neutralized, apply passing pressure immediately to prevent guard recovery
Movement Economy: Minimal wasted motion - DLR can punish inefficient movement with sweeps and transitions to more dominant guard variations
Passing Chains: Link multiple passing attempts together rather than forcing a single technique, as DLR rewards patient defenders who can stop isolated attacks

common_errors.error: Leaning forward over opponent with poor posture and head position ahead of hips
common_errors.consequence: DLR guard's primary threat is off-balancing you forward using the hook and grip combination. Poor posture makes these sweeps high-percentage, resulting in you being swept and guard player achieving top position or back take
common_errors.correction: Maintain upright posture with chest up and hips back. Your head should be over or slightly behind your hips, not leaning forward. Think about sitting back into their guard rather than leaning over them. Strong core engagement prevents being pulled forward

common_errors.error: Allowing opponent to maintain perpendicular hip angle throughout passing sequence
common_errors.consequence: DLR guard is most effective when bottom player's hips are angled perpendicular to you. This angle creates maximum sweep leverage and berimbolo entry opportunities. Allowing them to maintain it makes passing extremely difficult
common_errors.correction: Flatten their hips by pressuring their non-hooked leg toward the mat, or control their hips directly with hand grips. Force them to face you more squarely, which nullifies much of DLR's sweeping power. Their hips should be flat or at least not perfectly angled

common_errors.error: Ignoring grip fighting and allowing opponent to maintain strong ankle or pants grips
common_errors.consequence: The ankle/pants grip combined with the DLR hook creates a powerful control system. Without addressing grips, even perfect posture won't prevent sweeps or off-balancing
common_errors.correction: Immediately strip the ankle grip using your free hand, or secure a counter-grip on their collar or lapel to break their posture. If you can't strip it immediately, use your grips to control their upper body and limit their ability to use the ankle grip effectively

common_errors.error: Standing too close to opponent and allowing them to maintain compact guard structure
common_errors.consequence: DLR is most dangerous at mid-range where the hook and grips create optimal leverage. Standing too close allows them to maintain this ideal distance while limiting your passing options
common_errors.correction: Create distance first by backing away and extending their legs, or close distance completely by smashing into them. Avoid the mid-range danger zone where DLR thrives. Either make them extend (weakening their structure) or collapse the space entirely (removing hook effectiveness)

common_errors.error: Using tentative, half-committed passing attempts without full commitment to direction
common_errors.consequence: DLR rewards patient guard players who can read telegraphed movements. Tentative passing gives them time to adjust, reset grips, and execute sweeps or transitions
common_errors.correction: Once you've chosen a passing direction, commit fully with explosive movement and proper grips. If you're going to pass right, drive hard right. If you're going to backstep, backstep decisively. Hesitation in the middle of a pass is when you're most vulnerable

common_errors.error: Neglecting to control or pressure the non-hooked leg during passing attempts
common_errors.consequence: The free leg can create frames, establish new guards (lasso, spider, reverse DLR), or help the bottom player recover position. Ignoring it allows easy guard retention and recovery
common_errors.correction: Pin the non-hooked leg to the mat with your shin or hand, or control it with grips as you pass. This leg is their primary tool for creating distance and establishing secondary guard layers. Neutralizing it significantly improves passing success

training_drills.name: DLR Hook Removal Drill
training_drills.description: Partner establishes DLR hook with ankle grip. Top player practices three different hook removal methods: backstep to remove hook, pressure non-hooked leg across body while circling away from hook, and forward pressure to flatten hips and strip hook. Focus on maintaining posture throughout. Reset after each successful removal.

training_drills.name: Grip Fighting Flow Drill
training_drills.description: Bottom player establishes DLR with various grips (ankle, pants, belt, collar). Top player drills grip strips, counter-grips, and grip-fighting sequences while maintaining good posture and base. Bottom player actively fights to maintain grips. Practice transitions from successful grip breaks into passing entries.

training_drills.name: DLR Passing Chains Drill
training_drills.description: Partner plays active DLR guard with full resistance. Top player drills passing chains: start with toreando, if blocked flow to knee slice, if blocked flow to leg drag, if blocked flow to X-pass. Focus on reading bottom player's defensive reactions and smoothly chaining between passing options without resetting.

training_drills.name: Berimbolo Defense Drill
training_drills.description: Bottom player attempts berimbolo entries from DLR at 75% intensity. Top player practices recognition and counters: posting far leg, controlling near hip, transitioning to leg attacks, or executing stack passes. Emphasize early recognition of inversion and immediate defensive response.

training_drills.name: Positional Sparring: DLR Top Only
training_drills.description: Start in DLR guard top position. Top player's goal is to pass to side control or better within 2 minutes. Bottom player uses full DLR arsenal including sweeps, berimbolo, and guard transitions. Reset if bottom player sweeps or if top player passes. Track success rate over 5 rounds.

expert_insights.danaher: De La Riva guard presents a fascinating biomechanical problem that requires systematic understanding to solve consistently. The DLR hook creates a mechanical disadvantage by establishing a fulcrum point behind your leg combined with grip-based pulling force, creating rotational leverage that can off-balance even the most athletic practitioners if proper countermeasures aren't employed. The key insight is that DLR operates on a principle of angular control - the bottom player seeks to maintain a perpendicular hip angle relative to your torso, which maximizes their leverage while minimizing yours. Your primary objective isn't simply to pass, but rather to first neutralize this angular advantage by flattening their hips or forcing them to face you squarely. Once you've removed the perpendicular angle, the DLR hook loses most of its sweeping power and becomes merely a positional inconvenience rather than a serious threat. The secondary consideration is grip control - the ankle or pants grip provides the pulling force that, when combined with the hook's pushing force, creates the scissoring action that sweeps you. Strip this grip and you've removed half the equation. Modern DLR passing has evolved to include leg entanglement opportunities, particularly when the opponent inverts for berimbolo attempts, creating windows for saddle entries that can result in immediate submissions. The most effective passers treat DLR not as a single position to overcome, but as a dynamic system with multiple states, each requiring specific technical solutions based on hip angle, grip configuration, and the opponent's immediate intentions.
expert_insights.gordon_ryan: I pass DLR by immediately attacking the hook leg with aggressive intention and technical precision. My approach is to grab that shin and either backstep explosively to remove the hook and take the back, or smash it across their body for a leg drag that leads directly to passing opportunities. The key is being explosive and committed - tentative DLR passing gets you swept every time because you're stuck in the danger zone where their leverage is maximum. I also like creating distance first, letting them extend their legs and structure, then diving in hard with the pass when their structure is stretched and they can't generate the same power with the hook. DLR is dangerous at mid-range but weak at both close range where you can smash and pressure, and far range where they're extended and their hook loses effectiveness. Another thing I focus on heavily is not allowing them to establish their rhythm and grips. I'm constantly stripping grips, changing my stance, and forcing them to adjust. If they do get me off-balance, I have trained responses - immediate base recovery, posting the far leg, or transitioning to leg attacks if they invert. In competition, I've found that most DLR players have predictable patterns - they'll either try to sweep forward, attempt berimbolo, or transition to X-guard or single leg X. Once you recognize which pattern they prefer, you can anticipate and counter before they fully commit. The best DLR passers are proactive, not reactive - you dictate the engagement, not them.
expert_insights.eddie_bravo: DLR can be a nightmare if you don't know what you're doing, but once you understand the mechanics it becomes very manageable. In 10th Planet, we drill specific DLR counters extensively because so many competitors use it at the highest levels. The main thing is don't let them establish their rhythm and control. Pressure their non-hooked leg immediately, strip grips aggressively, and don't give them time to set up berimbolo or sweep entries. One thing I teach is to think about DLR as a position where time is your enemy - the longer you stay in it, the more opportunities they have to sweep or attack. So your mentality should be constant forward progress toward passing, not cautious position holding. If they do get you off-balance, be ready to sprawl or base out immediately with trained reactions. We also look for unconventional counters like transitioning to leg attacks when they invert, or using their DLR hook against them by stepping over and applying pressure to create leg entanglements. DLR rewards patience from the bottom but punishes hesitation from the top. You need to be aggressive, technical, and willing to engage rather than trying to maintain safe distance. The other key is having multiple passing options ready - if your toreando gets shut down, immediately flow to knee slice or leg drag. Chain your passes together and don't let them reset. Most people fail at DLR passing because they commit to one technique and force it even when it's not working. Be fluid, recognize when something isn't there, and smoothly transition to your next option.
